title: Why 90% utilization breaks teams: the non-linear cost of running without slack
summary: Using a web-server analogy, Jason Cohen argues that running people and teams near full capacity makes them brittle. Variation and interruption are inevitable, so teams need slack and should reserve high-gear surges for short, justified periods.

principles.text: Running at 90% utilization makes a system brittle: normal variation alone pushes it past capacity.
principles.quote: Even normal variations in traffic will drive the server past its capacity. The average time to respond to a request will skyrocket, and often requests will be dropped altogether.

principles.text: Pooling at 70% across a team still fails when one member drops out; redundancy needs real spare capacity.
principles.quote: The 2 remaining servers now have to deal with 2.1 servers' worth of traffic. Both are at 105% capacity, and we're back to broken and brittle.

principles.text: Overloaded people don't absorb shocks; they pass them on, causing cascading failure across the org.
principles.quote: Since they are over capacity, rather than absorb the spike, they too will ripple the problem to others--a cascade like the run-away chain reaction of an atom bomb.

principles.text: High utilization costs output, not just wellbeing, because of constant context-switching and interruption.
principles.quote: This condition is a combination of frequent context-switching and interruption--the Twin Enemies of productivity.

principles.text: Variation is inevitable, so design work-styles to be resilient to it rather than trying to plan it away.
principles.quote: you need to build a system that assumes variation and interruption, and design your personal and team's work-style to be resilient to that variation.

principles.text: Stay in a safe zone most of the time; allow surges only briefly and for good cause, such as launches or time-bounded rallies.
principles.quote: The ideal is probably a situation where most of the time you're in the safe zone, with occasional surges into high gear for a short period of time and for good cause.
